title: The Necessity of  a Third Founding
author: https://hedgehogreview.com/contributors/james-davison-hunter
text:
How does a social order rooted in Enlightenment-era ideals and presuppositions survive and thrive in a post-Enlightenment age? This puzzle plays out most urgently in the institutions of modern democracy, but we should not conclude that it concerns only democracy. It is a conundrum that is civilizational in scope, and the way we resolve it will have consequences in every sphere of individual and social life for generations to come.

Neither the predicament nor the way we might address it is self-evident. This is so because most people experience the evolution of the modern West as a linear progression marked by the increasing velocity of its own defining features. There appears to be a line of continuity running through the scientific, technical, and organizational rationality that has long defined the modern era. The same can be said of the multiplicity of human cultures and traditions modernity brought together. By this reading, the only thing that has really changed is quantitative: We have more of what we think constitutes modernity—all of which arrives at a faster and faster pace. The “modern” we experience today represents the expansion, intensification, and acceleration of those features of the “modern”—including its attendant problems—first experienced by Europeans in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.11xHartmut Rosa, Social Acceleration: A New Theory of Modernity (New York, NY: Columbia University Press, 2015).

It’s a compelling story and one that maps on to our sense of the long arc of the modern world. But what appears to be continuity conceals what is, in fact, a rupture in the social order, a rupture of world-historical consequence. To understand this rupture, we need to recall what the Enlightenment accomplished.

It is a commonplace that modernity, and the great democratic revolutions of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries that were its offspring, were underwritten by an intellectual and cultural revolution. The often-told story is that the Enlightenment was, very simply, the triumph of secular reason over traditional and religious ways of thought and social life. That account is, of course, a gross simplification. Far closer to the truth would be to say that the Enlightenment emerged as a historically contingent, hybrid cosmology drawing from an array of cultural sources. Across national contexts, this cosmology varied according to locally inflected combinations of the rich and assorted traditions of Roman and Greek antiquity, Catholicism, Protestantism, Judaism, early-modern natural law, and new, empirically grounded science, including a science of politics, seeking to establish rules of order for secular states no longer governed by divine right. Reflecting the diverse ways in which such sources were combined, “enlightenment” in Paris looked very different from “enlightenment” in London, Edinburgh, and Berlin, and all of these looked very different from what was found in Boston, Philadelphia, or Charlottesville.

The contingencies of place mattered. The American Founding emerged from a society marked by fissures within religious faith, economic interest, political allegiance, and, of course, region, race, and ethnicity. The struggle for power, often violent, was never incidental to these tensions and conflicts; nor were the consequences of those struggles benign.

For all of that, difference and conflict did not exhaust the cultural reality of the Founding. Americans quarreled within a moral world they substantially shared. Neither uniform nor uncontested, that moral order provided enough commonalities—of language, of norms, of aspirations—to make disagreement politically intelligible and even productive. The distinctive achievement of the American Enlightenment consisted in this generative capacity. It furnished arguments for resistance to the authority of the British Crown and, later, a framework of peaceable partisan disagreement, supplying, in Bernard Bailyn’s phrase, a “harmonizing force” through which otherwise antagonistic groups could imagine themselves as participants in a common national enterprise.

All of this was possible in large part because the Enlightenment in America was neither simply secular in the way some have claimed nor religious in the ways others have asserted. It was a hybrid that was rooted in the inherited theological patchwork of Christianity—largely Protestant or Reformed in origins, latitudinarian in observances, and often deistic or theistic in orientation—that allowed broad interpretation within a diverse population.

The categories of providence, vocation, charity, moral agency, and eschatological hope became a moral architecture for talking about republican virtue, citizenship, natural rights, public duty, historical progress, civic improvement, and national identity. Biblical obligation and republican virtue, considered by many at the time to be the same, placed claims on private interest and directed it, however imperfectly, toward public ends. Rather than repudiating Christianity’s central moral categories and energies, America’s hybrid Enlightenment revised and relocated them. The result was neither a disguised Christianity nor a fully secular moral order but an evolving synthesis in which religious and rationalist sources continued to shape and reinforce one another.

Within this cultural fusion, ideals such as liberty, equality, justice, and toleration acquired special prominence. Their meanings were contested and their application was radically and tragically uneven. Americans disagreed fiercely over what these ideals entailed, but the disagreement itself testified to their authority and proved they were not merely rhetorical ornaments. They carried enough substantive force to organize political argument, to sustain an emergent understanding of citizenship in a new nation, and to inspire generations of nation building.

In my most recent book, Democracy and Solidarity, I tell the story of America’s hybrid Enlightenment and how it evolved in fits and starts during the previous two centuries by “working through” deep contradictions inherent within itself—namely, the promise of freedom, equality, fairness, and toleration, and the denial of these moral and political goods to large swaths of its people. The long, hard, and always contested process of working through these fundamentally ethical inconsistencies often dramatically altered the character of the hybrid Enlightenment, even while leaving its fundamental propositions and claims recognizable to succeeding generations. It continued to provide the sources of national solidarity.

At least until recent decades.

Epistemic and Moral Authority

There are clear signs that we are now in a period of exhaustion. The repeatedly worked-through sources of the hybrid Enlightenment are now largely depleted and lack the binding authority they once had in public and political affairs. For some, those sources have faded from memory. For others, they have been recast and corrupted in service to partisan interests. For still others, they are seen as the original source of the nation’s failures and should be repudiated altogether. Whatever the reason, they have lost their compelling force as sources of shared public meaning, identity, and solidarity.

We now live in a world in which no account of truth or the good commands broad deference or respect. The collapse of trust in institutional authority reflects and contributes to this loss. While religion no longer provides a common epistemic, metaphysical, or even ethical horizon, autonomous reason does no better.

Consider how cultural authority has dissipated in two historically prominent areas of American society and culture, each with vital and organic ties to the hybrid Enlightenment: biblical authority and scientific authority.

Evangelicalism provides a fascinating case of what has happened to biblical authority. Mainstream evangelical Christianity formally holds to a theological orthodoxy that is, by its own account, closest to the orthodoxy of the Puritan and common Reformed Protestantism of the early nineteenth century. As a whole, evangelicals believe that it was their tradition that provided much of the animating moral and religious energy for the nation’s Founding and growth. By this account, America was a Christian nation, and, indeed, its leading institutions, not least its laws and its courts, its educational system, its colleges and universities, and its greatest reform movements reflected a conspicuous Protestant character. In turn, its leaders and votaries enjoyed the respect and influence that comes with the hegemonic influence of their beliefs.

Over the past century, of course, the tradition and the institutions that carry such respected authority have been marginalized, its leading ideas and beliefs ridiculed, and many of its most respected leaders defamed. Outside its own enclave, evangelical Christianity provides little credible authority in the intellectual or moral life of the nation. Evangelicalism not only sits on the periphery of the social order, but it also carries a stigma of opprobrium. This is why so many evangelical Christians today are so resentful of the secularizing turn of the country, especially within the country’s elite and elite institutions. As a movement, evangelicalism tells a story of collective injury, one rooted in disrespect and contempt for all they hold sacred and all their tradition has contributed to the nation. This marginalization has predictably led to resentment, both widely shared and deeply visceral. That sense of grievance has in turn fueled the politicization of evangelicalism, to the extent that many Americans now believe the word evangelical is more a political label than a religious one.

This is all well-known. The more interesting story is how the authority of evangelical belief has declined even within its own subcultural enclave. As with the Reform tradition of the sixteenth century, evangelicals continue to boast of a faith grounded in “the inspired, only infallible, authoritative Word of God.”22xFrom the Statement of Faith of the National Association of Evangelicals; https://www.nae.org/statement-of-faith/. Retrieved August 7, 2026. Rooted in their adherence to biblical truth, evangelicals to this day continue to affirm the traditional creeds of sin, sanctification, and eternal salvation through the death and resurrection of Jesus of Nazareth. Yet beneath this continuity, something more fundamental has changed.

Biblical authority has increasingly taken a subjectivist and therapeutic turn. Scripture continues to be acknowledged as authoritative in principle, but it has largely lost its capacity to confront believers as an objective authority standing over the self—making claims that command obedience independent of personal preference, emotional need, or lived experience. Instead, its meaning is increasingly filtered through the circumstances of the individual: the search for personal fulfillment, emotional healing, victorious living, abundant life, and the like.

The same shift extends beyond Scripture to the authority of pastors, priests, and theologians. Their words are no longer received simply because they faithfully expound the biblical text. Their authority is mediated through the question, What does this mean to me? In itself, this seems unremarkable. The difficulty arises when personal meaning becomes the final court of adjudication. What Scripture means for one believer need not mean the same for another, and once authority is relocated to subjective experience, shared interpretation and common understanding become increasingly difficult, perhaps impossible to sustain.

The language of historic evangelical orthodoxy may largely remain, but its center of gravity has shifted. Biblical revelation has not been explicitly rejected, though its authority has been subtly relocated. What once confronted the believer as an objective claim upon the self now becomes authoritative only insofar as it aligns with the needs and experiences of the self.33xAll of this is laid out conceptually and empirically in some of my earlier work: See Evangelicalism: The Coming Generation (Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Press, 1987) and “Subjectivization and the New Evangelical Theodicy,” Journal for the Scientific Study of Religion, vol. 21, no. 1 (March 1982), 39–47; https://www.jstor.org/stable/1385568.  In Karl Barth’s helpful phrase, it has lost its “binding address.”

Surely if this kind of subtle transformation of biblical authority has been happening in one of the most historically and doctrinally orthodox religious traditions in America, it is very likely happening throughout in the expansive mosaic of American religion, and even beyond.

One of those authoritative sources beyond religion is, of course, science, and while the trust and deference it commands remain strong in certain contexts, the standing of science as an authoritative arbiter of factual disputes has been severely damaged by its subordination to the partisanship of the culture war. As the COVID-19 pandemic made painfully clear, both sides of the cultural divide use science and scientific facts for their own purposes, with the net effect of undermining the institution as a whole.

But what is perhaps more interesting than the ideological uses of science is the story of the larger purposes of science within modernity, because here too we find an internal transformation of its own authority.

The story begins with the early-modern quest to find a scientific foundation for morality, a search that occupied the minds of some of Europe’s greatest philosophers—from Hugo Grotius and John Locke to Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill. It is no coincidence that these figures were also among the most influential political philosophers of their age. They recognized that the possibility of a liberalizing political order required a deeper cultural authority capable of sustaining shared understandings of justice, the good, and the obligations of citizenship. Could science, relying largely on its empirical methods (though not entirely abandoning the religious or metaphysical conviction of an ordered and orderly universe), effectively provide an alternative magisterium on which human flourishing and a liberal democratic order be established? Could it become the foundation of a just and humane social order?44xMy colleague Paul Nedelisky and I tell this story in Science and the Good: The Tragic Quest for the Foundations of Morality (New Haven, CT: Yale University Press, 2018).

Time after time, the quest to derive truth and ethical direction from the inductive, reductive, and empirical methods of science have fallen tragically short—and even, in some cases, led to some of the greatest enormities of modern history. Consider where the promise of eugenics led, and not only in Hitler’s Germany. Yet five hundred years after its inauguration, the quest continues, even as its largest truth claims have been challenged by some of the leading lights of modern philosophy. Nevertheless, the late twentieth century witnessed the birth of a new and reinvigorated effort to establish a comprehensive science of morality, this one advanced by sociobiologists, evolutionary psychologists, neuroscientists, and others. The new moral science also failed, but this time over the challenge of definition and the challenge of demonstration: The more morality was defined in an empirically measurable way, the less it resembled morality as it is actually experienced in social life; conversely, the more faithful the definition of morality was to human experience, the less amenable it became to empirical measurement. It still turns out, as the philosopher David Hume put it, you can’t derive “an ought from an is.”

Yet something very profound also transpired in this latest revival. The natural philosophers of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries sought a scientific account of morality because they still assumed that an objective moral order existed and could, in principle, be discovered. Their project unfolded within a metaphysical world still shaped by Aristotelian and Christian assumptions about the intelligibility and normativity of nature. The question was not whether objective moral truth existed but how it might best be known.

Four centuries later, however, the metaphysical landscape had been transformed by the very success of modern science. Aristotelian teleology had given way to a thoroughly naturalistic understanding of the world, one that recognized no intrinsic purposes, ends, or moral order within nature itself. Under the conditions of this “disenchanted naturalism,” the original ambition of moral science could no longer be sustained. Science can illuminate the consequences of our actions and help us achieve the ends we choose, but it cannot establish which ends are worth pursuing or why they should be regarded as objectively binding. Those judgments necessarily depend on moral commitments that lie outside the competence of science. Modern moral science therefore inherited the aspirations of the early Enlightenment while abandoning the metaphysical assumptions that once made those aspirations coherent.

The questions are, then, where do these moral commitments originate and by what authority do they command assent. Within a broadly naturalistic framework, they cannot arise from nature itself, for nature is understood to possess neither intrinsic purposes nor normative ends. They cannot be derived from science, for science describes the world as it is but cannot determine how it ought to be. At most, science can clarify the likely consequences of pursuing one set of ends rather than another.

The result is a profound inversion of the original project. What began as the search for an objective scientific foundation for morality now rests on moral commitments that science itself cannot justify. Those commitments are typically located instead in individual preference, emotional intuition, evolutionary inheritance, cultural tradition, democratic deliberation, or social consensus. Each may provide reasons for action, but none can establish that its moral claims are objectively true or universally binding. At best, they express what particular persons or communities happen to value under particular social and historical circumstances.

Modern moral science therefore does not so much discover moral truth as presuppose moral commitments whose authority lies elsewhere. The quest that began with the hope of placing morality on the firm foundation of science thus concludes by relocating moral authority to the very realm of subjective human preference and social contingency that the early-modern project sought to transcend.

The Broader Problem

Taken together, these two stories illustrate a broader transformation in the moral architecture of modern culture. Neither biblical revelation nor scientific reason now provides a comprehensive vision for the good, and neither commands the kind of public authority once imagined for it. The same can be said for any other authoritative claims: Political authority is dismissed as partisan, professional authority as self-interested, journalistic authority as ideological, and judicial authority as biased. In every sphere, authoritative claims are increasingly subjected to the prior judgment of an autonomous self. The question is no longer What is true? or By what authority? but What seems true to me and to those with whom I identify? That subtle but decisive shift may be among the defining cultural achievements—and failures—of late modernity.

Americans continue to invoke justice, freedom, equality, dignity, rights, tolerance, and inclusion. Yet these words no longer inhabit a common moral universe. Their meanings are increasingly defined within rival traditions of interpretation, each with its own assumptions about reality, authority, and the good. Under these conditions, disagreement rarely concerns policy alone. Every claim to truth or justice is met with suspicion; every institution is presumed to conceal interests; every opponent is assumed to argue in bad faith.

The digital revolution has vastly accelerated this fragmenting dynamic. The Internet promised to democratize knowledge by giving everyone access to information. Instead, it overwhelmed the public square with more information than anyone could reasonably evaluate and rewarded those most successful at attracting attention rather than pursuing truth. Algorithms amplify outrage rather than judgment. Markets reward engagement rather than accuracy. Political entrepreneurs traffic in resentment because resentment mobilizes. In such an environment, misinformation is not an accident but a business model or a political strategy.

The consequence is a kind of epistemic anarchy. Rumor, myth, and conspiracy theories flourish because they accomplish something that fractured public culture no longer can: They render the world intelligible. They identify hidden causes, explain suffering, expose enemies, and restore a sense of moral clarity to people who experience the world as increasingly confusing and unstable. Their persuasive force lies less in the evidence they marshal than in the meaning they provide. This is why fact-checking, though necessary, is generally beside the point. Where there is no agreement about legitimate authority or common standards of evidence, refutation itself is easily interpreted as yet another attempt to dominate and control.

A society that cannot agree about truth cannot easily sustain a common story about itself. For much of American history, biblical and secular millennialism—however flawed, exclusionary, and sometimes destructive—provided such a story. They located the American experiment within a larger narrative of purpose and gave civic life a shared horizon of hope. Citizens disagreed profoundly about how that promise should be realized, but they largely agreed that history possessed direction and that the nation’s future mattered.

But we no longer have such a narrative. History retains force, as the political scientist Wendy Brown observed, but it has lost direction. Without a broadly shared account of the future, politics becomes organized less around what can be built together than around what must be resisted or destroyed. The resulting visions of national purpose are increasingly sectarian: fantasies of restoration, ideological purification, Christian nationalism, revolutionary progressivism, or technological utopianism. Each offers its adherents identity, solidarity, and emotional reassurance. None has demonstrated the capacity to furnish a common future spacious enough to sustain a democratic people in all its diversity.

Toward Nihilism

Whatever else one may say about it, this historical and cultural environment meets textbook definitions of what Friedrich Nietzsche called “passive nihilism.”55xNietzsche distinguished between passive and active nihilism as two responses to the collapse of transcendent authority. Passive nihilism retreats into resignation, comfort, and the diminished aspirations of the “last man.” Active nihilism, by contrast, destroys inherited values in anticipation of creating new ones.

By nihilism, I do not mean decadence, despair, or the rejection of all moral belief. I mean a condition in which a society’s inherited sources of truth, value, and purpose lose their power to bind. Their language survives. People continue to invoke God, justice, rights, dignity, truth, freedom, and democracy. They continue to worship in churches, synagogues, mosques, and temples—or pursue newer forms of spirituality. Yet the organization of public life increasingly proceeds as though transcendence, truth, and common purpose were at best decorative and at worst obstructive.66xAlasdair MacIntyre, After Virtue: A Study in Moral Theory, third edition (Notre Dame, IN: University of Notre Dame Press, 2007); Émile Durkheim, Suicide: A Study in Sociology, trans. John A. Spaulding and George Simpson (New York, NY: Free Press, 1951).

Nietzsche saw this with singular clarity. He understood that the “death of God” was not principally a theological claim but a cultural diagnosis, a way of inhabiting the world after the weakening or collapse of any and all “god-terms” by which societies once named ultimate reality and judged the good. “What does nihilism mean? That the highest values devalue themselves,” he wrote. “The aim is lacking; ‘why?’ finds no answer.”77xFriedrich Nietzsche, The Will to Power, trans. Walter Kaufmann and R.J. Hollingdale (New York, NY: Vintage, 1968), 2; Friedrich Nietzsche, The Gay Science, trans. Walter Kaufmann (New York, NY: Vintage, 1974), 125.  The consequence is not the disappearance of values but their fragmentation. Moral languages multiply even as their authority diminishes. Convictions remain, but they no longer rest upon a shared account of reality or a common standard of judgment.

This helps explain one of the central paradoxes of late modernity. Never before have human beings possessed greater scientific knowledge, technological power, material abundance, or freedom of choice. Yet none of these achievements tells us what they are for. Science expands our power but cannot determine its proper ends. Markets multiply wealth but cannot define the good life. Information circulates globally, yet no corresponding moral or political authority exists to direct collective action toward common purposes. Our collective capacities have grown; our collective wisdom has not kept pace.

The paradoxes reach into personal experience as well. We have become extraordinarily adept at criticism. We can interrogate, deconstruct, and expose nearly every inherited belief, institution, and tradition. Yet these critical capacities are unmatched by an equal ability to affirm, commit, or sacrifice for ends larger than ourselves. We imagine different ways of living but possess no shared standard by which to judge whether one way is better than another. We enjoy unprecedented freedom to choose but little confidence that our choices matter in any ultimate sense, a sense other than what serves our own personal interests or comforts.88xMy colleagues and I expounded on this theme in the Vision Statement of the Institute for Advanced Studies in Culture; https://iasculture.org/vision/.

At the same time, the recovery of older certainties appears neither simple nor innocent. Absolutes evoke fear because they are remembered as instruments of domination, exclusion, and violence. The result is a culture suspended between the desire for moral substance and the dread of moral coercion. We yearn for convictions strong enough to sustain a common world yet recoil from the forms of authority by which such convictions were once secured.

Culture War as a Historical Marker

This, in short, is the rupture concealed by the narrative of continuity. And within it we find the source and larger meaning of the culture war.

In 1885, in the opening aphorism of Book One of what became The Will to Power, Nietzsche wrote that “Nihilism stands at the door: whence comes this most gruesome of all guests to us?”99xFriedrich Nietzsche, The Will to Power, trans. Walter Kaufmann and R.J. Hollingdale.  The sociologist Philip Rieff responded nearly a century later, in 1981, by arguing that “In America, as the successor to European culture, the door has been opened.” Now, nearly a half century later, it has become clear that this terrifying guest has made a home: in the public sphere as the will to power, and in the private sphere, in a therapeutic and consumerist culture of “last men” committed, above all, to personal well-being. Public and private are not opposites but complementary responses to the same cultural predicament.

The advance of nihilism, as Nietzsche describes it, provided the social and cultural conditions for the emergence of the culture war. The culture war, then, is the political manifestation of this rupture in the social order. In the absence of solidarity over the nature, meaning, and direction of the social order—however flawed—the culture war emerges as the struggle to impose a new solidarity, a new consensus, and a new hegemonic social order. It is, as I put it 1991, “the struggle to define America,” how we Americans will understand what America was, what it is, and what it will be. And make no mistake—it is a struggle for domination.

This is what the large number of critics in academic sociology and political science could not see. The political scientist Morris P. Fiorina, for example, declared, “The simple truth is that there is no culture war in the United States—no battle for the soul of America rages, at least none that most Americans are aware of.”1010xMorris P. Fiorina, Samuel J. Abrams, and Jeremy C. Pope, Culture War? The Myth of a Polarized America (New York, NY: Longman, 2005), 8. Fiorina goes on to add this qualification: “Certainly, one can find a few faux-warriors who engage in noisy skirmishes.… But their hatreds and battles are not shared by the great mass of the American people.” Fellow political scientist Alan Wolfe likewise denied the reality of a culture war: “there is little truth to the charge that middle-class Americans, divided by a culture war, have split into two hostile camps.”1111xAlan Wolfe, “The Culture War That Never Came,” in Is There a Culture War?, eds. Michael Cromartie and E.J. Dionne Jr. (Washington, DC: Brookings Institution Press, 2006); also Alan Wolfe, One Nation, After All: What Middle-Class Americans Really Think About God, Country, Family, Racism, Welfare, Immigration, Homosexuality, Work, the Right, the Left, and Each Other (New York, NY: Viking, 1998).  America, he wrote dispositively in the words of his book’s title, was One Nation, After All. And Paul DiMaggio and his colleagues at Princeton concluded similarly, in 1996, that there is “little evidence of polarization over the past two decades, with attitudes toward abortion and opinion differences between Republican and Democratic party identifiers the exceptional cases.”1212xPaul DiMaggio, John Evans, and Bethany Bryson, “Have Americans’ Social Attitudes Become More Polarized?” American Journal of Sociology, vol. 102, no. 3 (November 1996), 690–755; https://www.jstor.org/stable/2782461.

Yet my original argument in Culture Wars: The Struggle to Define America was never primarily about the polarization of public opinion over policies, as I suspect these and other critics knew. Rather, it concerned the emerging binary structure of moral authority embedded within an institutional contestation over the symbolic and normative ordering of the nation itself. Structure, not opinion—that is why the culture war has persisted and intensified.

Nor is the culture war confined to political parties, elected officials, or movement activists. Its principal battleground has become the institutions of civil society—universities, media outlets, philanthropic organizations, corporations, churches, and even scientific bodies. As these institutions have increasingly come to see themselves as participants in the culture war rather than as mediating authorities standing apart from it, they have steadily weakened their own credibility.

This is hardly the only reason public confidence has declined, but it is among the most consequential. To the extent that institutions subordinate their distinctive purposes to ideological objectives, they compromise the intrinsic goods that only they are uniquely positioned to provide and thereby erode the public trust upon which their authority depends. Donald Trump did not initiate this process, but he dramatically accelerated it by making distrust of institutional authority a governing principle. His most enduring legacy may prove not the falsehoods he told—destructive of public morality as those have been—but the normalization of the belief that no institution deserves public confidence except insofar as it advances one’s own political cause.

The critics of the “culture wars” hypothesis failed to grasp the deeper nature of the conflict, its larger historical significance, its extensive institutional range, and its most enduring political implications. It was a big miss. Likewise, they were slow to see how culture-war issues, often reduced to symbolic caricatures, were growing increasingly entwined with class conflicts, particularly the increasingly bitter hostility between highly educated and largely urban “elites” and the less credentialed working folks with their “love of guns and God.” And though passive nihilism created the conditions for the emergence of the culture war, it was only natural (or at least not surprising) that the culture war would eventually take on the character of an “active nihilism”—the will to power, the will to dominate, the will to annihilate.

The Necessity of a Third Founding

The first and second American Foundings emerged during periods of profound historical change, when the inherited symbolic and cultural order could no longer accommodate the demands of a changing world. As new social realities transformed the nation, political conflict intensified around competing visions of America’s identity and future. Our situation is different in its particulars but similar in its depth. Once again, the symbolic and moral order that underwrote the American experiment no longer sustains the weight placed upon it. The contradictions that animated the first two Foundings remain unresolved: Who belongs? What do freedom, equality, justice, and toleration require? How can people who differ fundamentally nevertheless constitute a common political community? These are not merely legal or institutional questions. They are questions of culture.

The dominant responses fail because they misunderstand the nature of the crisis. One seeks victory within the culture war by seeking to crush their political opponents. The other seeks better institutional design through procedural reform. The first intensifies the centrifugal forces pulling the republic apart. The second assumes that constitutions, laws, and procedures can generate the trust and solidarity upon which they themselves depend.

They cannot.

Written constitutions do not create the moral worlds that sustain them. Elections cannot manufacture mutual trust. Courts cannot legislate cultural legitimacy. Law can restrain conflict, but it cannot create the shared horizon of meaning that makes a peaceable pluralism and democratic self-government possible. As the legal scholar Robert Cover argued, every constitutional order presupposes a nomos—a normative world that gives law its intelligibility and authority. When that deeper constitution fragments, the formal constitution inevitably weakens with it.

This is the predicament of the present moment. American democracy is not failing merely because its politics have become polarized or its institutions dysfunctional. It is faltering because the cultural order that once sustained democratic legitimacy has largely unraveled and the hard question we face is whether we have the cultural resources to work through what divides us and to rebuild a nation.

That question, then, is larger than how to repair a political system. It is whether Americans, drawing on the most broadly shared truths from their diverse beliefs and traditions, can once again construct a moral order capacious enough to sustain both liberty and solidarity amid our deepest and most contentious differences. This calls not merely for another cycle of political reform. Rather, it calls for the longer and the deeper work of a Third Founding.
